text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Each year the Swedish state makes nearly two billion crowns in interest from student loans. The 1.2 million Swedes who have student loans pay interest rates far above the state's costs of taking up the loans.

- A power play between Peter Wallenberg and Claes Dahlback, the managing director of investment group Investor, stopped a merger between Swedish banks S-E-Banken and Nordbanken from taking place. The deal would have resulted in savings of two to 2.5 billion crowns, a stock market commentator writes. By not giving shareholders any information about the negotiations the board of S-E-Banken could turn down a favourable deal.

- Segregation of Swedes and immigrants is increasing. Since 1985 the number of immigrants living the the sections of Stockholm which already have the highest number of immigrants has risen. The biggest change has taken place in a part of Stockholm called Kista. In 1985 29 percent of Kista's residents were immigrants. This figure rose to 51 percent in 10 years.

- Sweden continues to lose competitiveness. The World Competitiveness Yearbook, published by the International Institiute for Management (IMD) in Switzerland, puts Sweden in 16th place in 1997 compared to 14th a year earlier. Both Scandinavian neighbours Norway and Denmark are above Sweden in the list, which puts the United States in first place.
- Published only on Fridays for the next three weeks because of summer holidays.
